  1. PostgreSQL Partial Index

    ✕
    This summary was generated using AI based on multiple online sources. To view the original source information, use the "Learn more" links.

    A partial index in PostgreSQL is an index built on a subset of table rows, defined by a WHERE clause (predicate). Only rows matching the condition are indexed, making the index smaller, faster to scan, and cheaper to maintain compared to a full index. This is especially useful when queries frequently target a specific subset of data.

    Key advantages include:

    • Reduced storage since irrelevant rows are excluded.

    • Faster queries for matching conditions due to smaller index size.

    • Lower write overhead because updates/inserts outside the predicate don’t affect the index.

    • -- Create partial index
      CREATE INDEX idx_customer_inactive
      ON customer(active)
      WHERE active = 0;

      -- Query that benefits from the partial index
      SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, email
      FROM customer
      WHERE active = 0;
      ✕
      Copy
      Copied!

      Here, only inactive customers are indexed, avoiding storage and maintenance for active ones.

    Best practices:

    • Match the WHERE clause in queries exactly to the index predicate for it to be used.

    • Use when the indexed subset is small and stable.

    • Avoid for high-selectivity conditions or volatile data patterns.

    • Don’t replace partitioning with many partial indexes; use table partitioning for large datasets.

    Partial indexes are a targeted optimization tool—most effective when you know your query patterns and data distribution well.
